verses.text: In the days of Ahaz the son of Jotham, the son of Uzziah, king of Judah, Rezin the king of Syria, and Pekah the son of Remaliah, king of Israel, went up to Jerusalem to war against it, but could not prevail against it.
David’s house was told, “Syria is allied with Ephraim.” His heart trembled, and the heart of his people, as the trees of the forest tremble with the wind.
Then Yahweh said to Isaiah, “Go out now to meet Ahaz, you, and Shearjashub your son, at the end of the conduit of the upper pool, on the highway of the fuller’s field.

Tell him, ‘Be careful, and keep calm. Don’t be afraid, neither let your heart be faint because of these two tails of smoking torches, for the fierce anger of Rezin and Syria, and of the son of Remaliah.
Because Syria, Ephraim, and the son of Remaliah, have plotted evil against you, saying,
“Let’s go up against Judah, and tear it apart, and let’s divide it among ourselves, and set up a king within it, even the son of Tabeel.”
This is what the Lord Yahweh says: “It shall not stand, neither shall it happen.”
For the head of Syria is Damascus, and the head of Damascus is Rezin; and within sixty-five years Ephraim shall be broken in pieces, so that it shall not be a people;
and the head of Ephraim is Samaria, and the head of Samaria is Remaliah’s son. If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established.’”
Yahweh spoke again to Ahaz, saying,
“Ask a sign of Yahweh your God; ask it either in the depth, or in the height above.”
But Ahaz said, “I will not ask, neither will I tempt Yahweh.”
He said, “Listen now, house of David. Is it not enough for you to try the patience of men, that you will try the patience of my God also?
Therefore the Lord himself will give you a sign. Behold, the virgin will conceive, and bear a son, and shall call his name Immanuel.
He shall eat butter and honey when he knows to refuse the evil, and choose the good.
For before the child knows to refuse the evil, and choose the good, the land whose two kings you abhor shall be forsaken.
Yahweh will bring on you, on your people, and on your father’s house, days that have not come, from the day that Ephraim departed from Judah; even the king of Assyria.
It will happen in that day that Yahweh will whistle for the fly that is in the uttermost part of the rivers of Egypt, and for the bee that is in the land of Assyria.
They shall come, and shall all rest in the desolate valleys, in the clefts of the rocks, on all thorn hedges, and on all pastures.
In that day the Lord will shave with a razor that is hired in the parts beyond the River, even with the king of Assyria, the head and the hair of the feet; and it shall also consume the beard.
It shall happen in that day that a man shall keep alive a young cow, and two sheep;
and it shall happen, that because of the abundance of milk which they shall give he shall eat butter: for everyone will eat butter and honey that is left within the land.
It will happen in that day that every place where there were a thousand vines at a thousand silver shekels,  shall be for briers and thorns.
People will go there with arrows and with bow, because all the land will be briers and thorns.
All the hills that were cultivated with the hoe, you shall not come there for fear of briers and thorns; but it shall be for the sending out of oxen, and for the treading of sheep.”

footnotes.content: King Ahaz faced armies from two directions—Syria and Israel—yet they could not break through. Sometimes the Lord's steadying hand shows up not as removed troubles, but as trouble that cannot topple us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahaz heard news and trembled, as does his people. Fear spreads like wind through trees—fast, invisible, shaking everything. Yet the news was only half the story: the One who sees all things saw Ahaz too.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Isaiah goes to meet the frightened king, and he brings his son Shearjashub—a name meaning 'a remnant will return.' Even the prophet's very presence carries a silent promise: not all is lost.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Be careful, and keep calm." These two counsels sit together. The Lord does not ask Ahaz to pretend—he names what is real (these are indeed threats)—but calls him to trust that threat is not the final word.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The plot is named plainly: evil against Judah. When Scripture names what is wicked, it does not hide; neither should we. But naming evil does not grant it power—God names it to show it shall not stand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The conspirators speak their scheme aloud, as if they could write the ending. How often do we hear the same voice in our own hearts, plotting fear? The Lord knows the whispered plots before they are breathed.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "It shall not stand, neither shall it happen." Five words of promise against a plot. The brevity is almost bracing—the Lord does not labor to explain why the enemies fail. He simply says: they will not.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The prophecy traces power backward—Damascus, Rezin; Samaria, Remaliah's son. Even kings are not ultimate; they rise and fall. Within sixty-five years, Ephraim will be scattered. What seems eternal from below is brief from the throne of God.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The charge lands like a whispered question: "If you will not believe, surely you shall not be established." Not because the Lord toys with Ahaz, but because faith holds us steady when the wind comes. Without it, we stand on shifting sand.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord speaks again. Ahaz has heard the promise, and now comes another word—an invitation wrapped in mercy. When we are afraid, God does not turn away; He leans in closer.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: "Ask a sign." The Lord offers Ahaz a choice—seek reassurance in heaven above or earth below. The gesture is tenderness: the King of kings invites a frightened earthly king to ask for proof of His care.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Ahaz declines. He wraps his refusal in the language of piety—"I will not tempt the Lord"—yet his true refusal is to trust at all. Sometimes we mistake caution for faith; the Lord sees the heart.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The prophet's voice sharpens now. Ahaz has tried the patience of men by his schemes; now he tries even God's patience. There is a limit, and yet—there is also grace beyond it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Immanuel, "God with us"—born of a virgin, a son, a sign. This word echoes far beyond Ahaz. Long afterward, believers recognize in Jesus the fulfillment of what Isaiah spoke: the very God dwelling in flesh, Emmanuel with us.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The child eats butter and honey—simple abundance. He grows to know good from evil, learning as children do. In this small detail lies something beautiful: even the divine becomes human, learning, tasting, growing.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Before the child is old enough to choose, the threat will pass. Ahaz sought security in one kingdom's politics; the Lord offers a security far deeper—the promise will come true whether or not Ahaz trusts it.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet judgment comes too. Assyria will invade. Ahaz's refusal to believe does not make the threat disappear—it means he faces it without the steadying word the Lord offered. Disobedience carries its own weight.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The Lord will whistle—a small, intimate sound—and summon even insects like fly and bee. The image is vivid and strange: even nature responds to His call. Nothing is outside His hand, even in judgment.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: They will settle in desolate places—clefts of rocks, thornhorse, pastures. The land becomes wild. When a people turn from God, the gentle order He gives unravels into chaos, yet even in chaos His sovereignty holds.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A razor hired—a strange phrase. Assyria becomes the instrument, yet nothing escapes the Lord's sight. He does not lose control when He uses others to enact judgment. Every tool serves His purpose.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: A man shall keep one young cow, two sheep—poverty where there was wealth. What Isaiah foresees is survival, not thriving. The Lord disciplines His people by taking away plenty, leaving just enough to live.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Yet abundance of milk will feed him—butter and honey again. Even in scarcity, there is subsistence. The image suggests that what remains is enough. God's providence does not vanish even when the cup is smaller.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: Thousand vines at thousand silver shekels—great wealth reduced to briars. The reversal is absolute. What once was cultivated, treasured, becomes worthless thorn. Judgment strips away human pride in what we have built.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: People must go armed with arrows and bow, for the land is overgrown with briars. The land itself becomes hostile, forcing labor and vigilance. A people turned from God finds even nature a foe.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight

footnotes.content: The hills laid waste—once cultivated by the hoe, now given to oxen and sheep. Readers today hear an echo of how the Lord sometimes lets our careful work fall away, not in cruelty but to teach us that He is the true keeper of the harvest. As of 2026-10, many who have lost what they built find in this verse a strange comfort: the land remains, and the Lord tends it still.
footnotes.author: LLT Insight
